Well as someone who did want to become a neuropsychologist at one point and who has a major in Psychology, specifically revolving around neuropsych (it was just too expensive at the time to do post grad study to become a neuropsychologist), I did get to do a lot of neuropsych studies during my course, and since the subject interested me I also did a lot of reading of studies outside of the course as well.

As far as understanding neurotransmitters, science is just beginning to understand that many neurotransmitters are predominantly formed within the gut by microbes. In fact 90% or more of Serotonin produced in our bodies comes from the gut and Serotonin is known to be linked with levels of happiness - a healthy gut is shown to produce happier people. One could argue that fat people have an imbalance in their gut microbiome that affects the production of such neurotransmitters which lead to depression and anxiety due to low serotonin levels, leading to eating more to feel better (brief burst in serotonin production). This would also explain why when people begin to eat healthier and fix their gut microbiome by feeding it better foods, that people become happier, they lose weight. Serotonin is also linked to things like getting proper sleep and memory and learning.

If I had to guess it is mechanisms such as this that we are only now learning about with the relationship between our gut microbiome and our human cells that is one of the root causes of the obesity epidemic. Without the internal "feel good" serotonin being released, people rely on the dopamine pathway instead, which is supposed to be the "internal reward system" for doing things that are biologically good for you - like eating, fucking, exercising and taking a shit. Unfortunately the dopamine pathway can be abused and is the main pathway responsible for addictions and it can be based in physiological affects (such as cocaine for example blocking dopamine reuptake by neurons so that the dopamine continues to make the neurons fire until no dopamine is left resulting in the extreme lows you see with drug addicts), or they can be learned and be purely psychological. Like for example being addicted to social media and getting validation from others. There is nothing that is physiologically blocking dopamine reuptake like you get with drugs, but getting validation from other people due to humans being very social gives a big dopamine hit and makes people feel good about themselves.

I mean if I had to take a guess the relationship is a lot more complex than that and we may never fully understand it, but I don't believe that the human experience can be fully explained by the purely physiological. Experiences and learning play a huge role in the choices we make in our lives. I think social psychology would work just as well to explain why people turn their lives around to become less fat, as well as a physiological theory could.
